caption:
Popular isn't the same as good.

Researchers at Texas A&M, the University of Texas at Austin and Purdue kept training four open models on short, popular Twitter/X posts.

Llama3 8B Instruct took it hardest. Its reasoning score fell from 72.1 to 57.2 as the junk share rose from 0% to 100%. Popularity tracked the damage better than length did.

The models skipped steps. The paper's "No Thinking" label appeared in 84% of failures under junk training.

Instruction data at 4.8 times the junk tokens didn't fully undo the damage. The best repaired models still trailed the baseline by 17.3 points on reasoning.

The deck builds each score as a stair's height.

The junk shares were doses in a training mix, not a reading of the internet. ChatGPT and Gemini aren't open source and weren't tested. Would a closed model skip the same steps?

#TexasAM #UTAustin #TrainingData
first_comment:
c6 The paper lists its affiliations as Texas A&M University, the University of Texas at Austin and Purdue University. https://arxiv.org/html/2510.13928v3
c16 The junk and control sets were drawn from 1 million public Twitter/X posts. https://arxiv.org/html/2510.13928v3
c18 Under the engagement measure, junk was posts under 30 tokens with popularity over 500, and control was posts over 100 tokens with zero popularity. https://arxiv.org/html/2510.13928v3
c19 The paper's popularity count is the total of a post's likes, retweets, replies and quotes. https://arxiv.org/html/2510.13928v3
c25 The four models tested were Llama3 8B Instruct, Qwen2.5 7B Instruct, Qwen2.5 0.5B Instruct and Qwen3 4B Thinking 2507. https://arxiv.org/html/2510.13928v3
c26 Each model was continually pre-trained on a junk and control mixture, then instruction tuned again on 5k Alpaca English examples. https://arxiv.org/html/2510.13928v3
c28 Under M1, ARC Challenge accuracy with chain of thought fell from 72.1 to 57.2 as the junk share rose from 0% to 100%. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13928
c30 The paper's dose response table reports Llama3 8B Instruct trained on varying mixtures of junk and control data. https://arxiv.org/html/2510.13928v3
c33 Under the engagement measure, ARC Challenge with chain of thought scored 57.2, 64.1, 69.3, 71.2 and 72.1, from all junk to no junk. Base scored 77.2. https://arxiv.org/html/2510.13928v3
c38 The paper identifies thought skipping as the main reasoning failure, with models increasingly truncating or skipping reasoning chains. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13928
c39 No Thinking appeared in over 70% of failures across all cases and in 84% under M1 junk. https://arxiv.org/html/2510.13928v3
c40 Within M1, a tweet's popularity was a better indicator of the effect than its length. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13928
c42 The repair tests started from Llama3 8B Instruct after 100% M1 junk training. https://arxiv.org/html/2510.13928v3
c44 Instruction data totaling 4.8 times the junk tokens still did not fully undo the damage. https://arxiv.org/html/2510.13928v3
c47 The best repaired models still trailed the baseline by 17.3% on ARC Challenge with chain of thought, 9% on RULER and 17.4% on AdvBench. https://arxiv.org/html/2510.13928v3
c57 All four models showed some dose response. Llama3 8B Instruct was the most sensitive to junk and Qwen3 4B the least. https://arxiv.org/html/2510.13928v3
c64 The junk ratios are doses within the training mixture, not estimates of how much of the internet is junk. https://arxiv.org/html/2510.13928v3
c65 The release says testing larger models such as ChatGPT or Gemini, which are not open source, is still needed. https://news.engineering.tamu.edu/news/2026/10/19/ai-models-can-get-brain-rot-too/
why_this_opening: The paper's sharpest result is that a post's popularity predicted the damage better than its length did, so the caption opens by correcting the habit of treating engagement as quality.
